title: Lesson 46: Multi-Org Architecture: When to Split, and Org-to-Org Integration Patterns
description: When a second Salesforce org is legitimate, when a split is an expensive dodge of a governance problem, and the patterns that connect orgs that must stay separate.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Multi-Org Architecture: When to Split, and Org-to-Org Integration Patterns”, which situation is a legitimate structural reason to split, and which reason does it replace?
options: A regulatory or compliance walled-garden requirement, which replaces a slow request backlog as a reason to give a line of business its own org.
The lines of business wanting their own space, which is met with a center of excellence, delegated administration, and tiered data architecture instead of a split.
A regulatory or compliance walled-garden requirement that sharing alone cannot satisfy, because the requirement is structural isolation and reviewability, not record visibility.
A desire for a faster-paced release cycle, which a second org delivers with no added integration cost.
questions.explanation: The legitimate split is the one where the wall itself is the requirement, giving a compliance burden its own isolated org and reviewable audit trail, which a sharing model controls visibility but cannot deliver.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Salesforce Connect with the cross-org adapter connects directly to another org’s data over the standard REST API without an intermediary web service, so a spoke can read hub master data with the hub’s permissions enforced.
Salesforce Connect’s cross-org adapter requires a middleware web service between the two orgs, which is why hub-and-spoke needs MuleSoft for every read path.
Platform events cross an org boundary on their own, so no relay is needed for an event published in one org to reach subscribers in another.
Salesforce-to-Salesforce is the recommended modern tool for new org-to-org integrations, because it is the only protocol that links records across two orgs.
questions.explanation: The cross-org adapter uses the platform’s REST API directly between the two orgs with no intermediary, and platform events stay org-scoped, so cross-org event delivery needs a relay bridge.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A multi-org estate shares one transaction across the boundary, so an update reflected in both orgs is atomic by design.
Duplicating canonical reference data into a spoke so it can change locally is a free way to gain autonomy without reconciling two sources of truth.

The two orgs do not share a transaction, so a cross-org integration is still an integration and needs the same idempotency, retry, and testing discipline as any external system, tolerating eventual consistency.
A single user who needs access to two orgs still consumes a single license, because Salesforce licenses a person, not an org.
questions.explanation: Neither org can participate in a transaction the other starts, so the design must tolerate a disagreement window; a user in two orgs consumes a license in each, and duplicated canonical data is a standing reconciliation obligation.
